q: Harbor Arts, an NFP, began the year with $800,000 of net assets with donor restrictions. During the year it received $300,000 of new donor-restricted gifts, earned $40,000 of unappropriated investment return on donor-restricted endowment funds, and satisfied purpose restrictions by spending $250,000 on the restricted programs. What are net assets with donor restrictions at year-end?
exp: Net assets with donor restrictions: $800,000 + $300,000 + $40,000 - $250,000 released = $890,000. Unappropriated return on a donor-restricted endowment stays with donor restrictions, so the $850,000 answer wrongly omits it.

q: An NFP spends donor-restricted cash on the program the donor specified. How is this reported in the statement of activities?
choices: As an expense reported directly in net assets with donor restrictions
As a reclassification that decreases net assets with donor restrictions and increases net assets without donor restrictions, with the expense reported in net assets without donor restrictions
As a reduction of the original contribution revenue in net assets with donor restrictions
As a prior-period adjustment to net assets with donor restrictions
exp: Satisfying a restriction is reported as net assets released from restrictions, a reclassification between the two classes, and all expenses are reported in net assets without donor restrictions (ASC 958-205-45). Expenses are never reported directly in the with-donor-restrictions class.

q: In December of Year 1, a donor made an unconditional promise to give River Clinic $100,000 at the end of each of the next five years with no stated use restriction. The present value of the payments is $379,000 and no allowance is needed. How should River Clinic report the promise in Year 1?
choices: $500,000 contribution revenue with donor restrictions
$379,000 contribution revenue without donor restrictions
$379,000 contribution revenue with donor restrictions
No revenue until each payment is received
exp: Unconditional promises are recognized when made, measured at present value, and amounts due in future periods carry an implied time restriction, so $379,000 is reported with donor restrictions. The $500,000 answer ignores discounting of multi-year pledges.

q: In Year 2, River Clinic records $22,000 of discount accretion on a multi-year unconditional pledge it recognized at present value in Year 1. How should the accretion be reported?
choices: As interest income in net assets without donor restrictions
As investment return, net of investment expenses
As a reduction of fundraising expense
As contribution revenue
exp: Accretion of the discount on a promise to give is reported as contribution revenue, in the net asset class of the original contribution (ASC 958-310). Treating it as interest income is the common mistake; the pledge is not a lending arrangement.

q: A foundation promises Elm Shelter $1 for every $1 Elm raises from other donors, up to $50,000, and the promise lapses for any unmatched amount after June 30 of next year. By December 31, Elm's year-end, it had raised $30,000 of qualifying gifts. How much contribution revenue from the foundation should Elm recognize this year?
exp: A matching grant is a conditional promise with a barrier and right of release; revenue is recognized as the barrier is overcome, here for the $30,000 matched so far. The $50,000 answer treats the full conditional promise as unconditional.

q: Under ASC 958-605 as amended by ASU 2018-08, a promise to give is conditional when the agreement contains which of the following?
choices: Any donor stipulation limiting the use of the assets
Both a barrier that must be overcome and a right of return of assets or right of release from the obligation
A payment schedule extending beyond one year
A requirement to report to the donor on how funds were spent
exp: A conditional contribution requires both a barrier (such as a measurable performance-related hurdle) and a right of return or release. A limitation on use alone is a donor restriction, not a condition, so the contribution is recognized now with donor restrictions.

q: A state agency awards a university $400,000 to research a public health issue. Results will be published publicly and the agency obtains no proprietary rights or other direct benefit. How should the university classify the award?
choices: Exchange transaction, because the agency selected the research topic
Exchange transaction recognized under ASC 606 as research is performed
Contribution, because the general public rather than the agency receives the benefit
Agency transaction recorded as a liability to the state
exp: Under ASU 2018-08, a transfer is an exchange only if the resource provider receives commensurate value; benefits to the general public do not count as commensurate value to the grantor, so the award is a contribution (often conditional). Choosing the topic does not make the agency a customer.

q: Members of Valley Museum pay $100 annual dues and receive free admission, a magazine and shop discounts with a total fair value of about $100. How should the museum account for the dues?
choices: As contribution revenue when the dues are received
As contribution revenue with donor restrictions released monthly
As an agency transaction with no revenue recognized
As exchange revenue recognized over the membership period
exp: When members receive benefits commensurate with the dues paid, the dues are an exchange transaction recognized as performance obligations are satisfied over the membership year. Only the portion of dues exceeding the value of benefits would be a contribution.

q: During the year, Pine Hospital received these donated services: a licensed electrician rewired a wing ($12,000 value), volunteers staffed the gift shop ($20,000 value), and a CPA prepared the annual information return for free ($6,000 value), a service Pine would otherwise have purchased. How much contributed services revenue should Pine recognize?
exp: Contributed services are recognized only if they create or enhance nonfinancial assets (the rewiring, $12,000) or require specialized skills, are provided by people with those skills and would otherwise be purchased (the CPA, $6,000): $12,000 + $6,000 = $18,000. Gift shop volunteering requires no specialized skill, so the $38,000 answer is wrong.

q: Under ASU 2020-07, how must an NFP present contributed nonfinancial assets such as donated food, equipment and services?
choices: Netted against the related program expenses on the statement of activities
As a separate line item in the statement of activities, apart from contributions of cash and other financial assets, with disaggregation by category in the notes
Only in the notes, with no amount recognized in the statement of activities
Combined with cash contributions in a single contributions line
exp: ASU 2020-07 requires gifts-in-kind to be presented as a separate line item and disaggregated by category, with disclosure of monetization or use policies, donor restrictions and valuation techniques. It did not change recognition, so disclosure-only treatment is wrong.

q: Oak Theater, an NFP, sold 400 tickets to its annual gala at $250 each. The fair value of the dinner and entertainment each attendee received was $90. How much contribution revenue should Oak recognize from ticket sales?
exp: Each ticket is part exchange and part contribution: 400 x ($250 - $90) = $64,000 contribution, and 400 x $90 = $36,000 exchange revenue. The $100,000 answer treats the full price as a gift and ignores the benefit attendees received.

q: A donor transfers $1,000,000 of securities to a charitable remainder annuity trust and names Lake College as trustee and remainder beneficiary. The trust pays the donor $50,000 a year for life; the present value of the expected annuity payments is $420,000. What contribution revenue should Lake College recognize at inception?
choices: $1,000,000 with donor restrictions
$580,000 without donor restrictions
$0 until the donor dies
$580,000 with donor restrictions
exp: As trustee, Lake recognizes the $1,000,000 of trust assets, a $420,000 annuity liability and the $580,000 difference as contribution revenue with donor restrictions, because the remainder is time-restricted until the trust terminates. Reporting it without donor restrictions ignores that time restriction.

q: A donor places $2,000,000 in a perpetual trust administered by an unrelated bank. Willow Shelter has an irrevocable right to receive the trust's income forever but will never receive the trust assets. How should Willow report the arrangement at inception?
choices: Recognize a beneficial interest and contribution revenue with donor restrictions, measured at fair value
Disclose the arrangement only, since the bank controls the assets
Recognize contribution revenue without donor restrictions only as income is received
Recognize a beneficial interest offset by a liability to the bank
exp: A beneficiary with an unconditional right to cash flows from a perpetual trust held by a third party recognizes its beneficial interest at fair value (usually the fair value of the trust assets) as contribution revenue with donor restrictions (perpetual). Recognizing only income as received ignores the unconditional right that already exists.

q: Under a charitable lead trust administered by a bank, Birch Hospital will receive $40,000 a year for ten years, after which the remaining trust assets go to the donor's children. How should Birch recognize the arrangement at inception?
choices: Contribution revenue equal to the full fair value of the trust assets
Contribution revenue with donor restrictions measured at the fair value of its beneficial interest, typically the present value of the expected payments
Contribution revenue without donor restrictions of $400,000
No recognition, because the remainder goes to the donor's heirs
exp: In a lead trust the NFP is entitled only to the lead payments, so it recognizes a beneficial interest equal to their present value as contribution revenue with donor restrictions (time-restricted until received). The undiscounted $400,000 ignores time value, and the full trust value includes the heirs' remainder.

q: A community foundation receives $75,000 from a donor with instructions to transfer it to a specific food bank. The foundation has no variance power. How should the foundation and the food bank report the transfer?
choices: The foundation recognizes contribution revenue; the food bank recognizes nothing until it receives cash
Both entities recognize $75,000 of contribution revenue
The foundation recognizes an asset and a liability; the food bank recognizes contribution revenue and a receivable
The foundation recognizes contribution revenue and a grant expense; the food bank discloses the gift
exp: Without variance power the foundation is an agent or intermediary, so it records the cash and a liability to the food bank, while the specified beneficiary recognizes the contribution and a receivable (ASC 958-605-25). Recognizing revenue at both entities would double count one gift.

q: A donor gives $75,000 to a community foundation, suggests that it go to a particular food bank, and explicitly grants the foundation unilateral power to redirect the gift to another beneficiary. How should the foundation report the receipt?
choices: As a liability to the suggested food bank
As an agency transaction disclosed in the notes only
As contribution revenue of the suggested food bank
As contribution revenue of the foundation
exp: Explicit variance power gives the foundation control over the assets, so the foundation recognizes the contribution and the suggested beneficiary does not. Recording a liability is the treatment when no variance power exists.

q: At June 30, Birch Services reports cash of $300,000 (including $40,000 a donor restricted for a building to be built in three years), receivables of $200,000 (of which $60,000 are due in 18 months) and investments of $900,000 (of which $700,000 is perpetual endowment corpus). No endowment appropriation is expected in the next year. What financial assets are available to meet general expenditures within one year?
exp: Available: cash $300,000 - $40,000 restricted = $260,000; receivables $200,000 - $60,000 = $140,000; investments $900,000 - $700,000 = $200,000; total $600,000. The $640,000 answer forgets the building-restricted cash, which cannot be used for general expenditures.

q: Which liquidity information does ASU 2016-14 require NFPs to provide?
choices: A classified statement of financial position separating current and noncurrent items
Qualitative information on how the entity manages liquid resources to meet cash needs for general expenditures within one year, and quantitative information on the availability of financial assets
A statement of cash flows prepared using the direct method
Liquidity ratios with comparisons to industry averages
exp: ASU 2016-14 requires qualitative disclosure of liquidity management and quantitative disclosure of financial assets available for general expenditures within one year of the balance sheet date. It does not require a classified balance sheet; sequencing by liquidity or other presentation remains acceptable.

q: Under current ASC 958 requirements, which NFPs must present an analysis of expenses by both function and nature?
choices: Only voluntary health and welfare entities
Only NFPs with public debt outstanding
All NFPs, in one location: the face of the statement of activities, a separate statement, or the notes
Only NFPs that elect to present an operating measure
exp: ASU 2016-14 extended the function-and-nature analysis to all NFPs and requires it in one location. Limiting it to voluntary health and welfare entities reflects the superseded rule, which is why that answer tempts candidates.

q: Maple Society mailed a brochure containing educational information about heart health and a request for donations, at a total cost of $80,000. The purpose and content criteria for joint activities are met, but the mailing list was selected solely on the basis of recipients' past giving. How should the $80,000 be reported?
choices: $40,000 program services and $40,000 fundraising
Allocated between program services and fundraising based on relative content
$80,000 program services
$80,000 fundraising
exp: Joint costs can be allocated to program services only if the purpose, audience and content criteria are all met; an audience chosen solely for likelihood of giving fails the audience criterion, so all costs are fundraising (ASC 958-720-45). Allocation is permitted only when all three criteria are met.

q: The fair value of Ash College's donor-restricted endowment fund falls to $900,000, below the $1,000,000 original gift amount the donor required to be maintained. How is the $100,000 deficiency reported?
choices: As a reduction of net assets with donor restrictions
As a reduction of net assets without donor restrictions
As a liability to the donor
In the notes only, with no effect on net assets
exp: Under ASU 2016-14, accumulated losses on underwater donor-restricted endowments reduce net assets with donor restrictions, with disclosure of the fair value, original gift amount and deficiency. Charging the shortfall to net assets without donor restrictions was the superseded practice.

q: The board of Cedar Hospice designates $500,000 of cash from unrestricted gifts as a quasi-endowment to be invested long term. How should these assets be classified?
choices: Net assets with donor restrictions, perpetual in nature
Net assets without donor restrictions, with board designations permitted on the face or in the notes
Net assets with donor restrictions, time-restricted
A separate third class of board-designated net assets
exp: Only donors create restrictions; a board designation is an internal decision the board can reverse, so the assets remain without donor restrictions, and the designation may be presented or disclosed. A separate third class does not exist under ASC 958.

q: In Year 1, Aspen Center received a $1,200,000 gift restricted to constructing a facility. Construction was paid in Year 2, and the facility was placed in service on January 1, Year 3, with a 30-year life. The donor did not specify how long the facility must be used. When are the restricted net assets released?
choices: $40,000 per year over 30 years beginning in Year 3
$1,200,000 in Year 1 when received
$1,200,000 in Year 3 when the facility is placed in service
$1,200,000 in Year 2 as construction costs are paid
exp: ASU 2016-14 requires the placed-in-service approach absent explicit donor stipulations, so the full $1,200,000 is released when the facility is placed in service in Year 3. Releasing over the useful life was an option eliminated by that standard.

q: In the statement of cash flows of an NFP, how should cash received from a donor restricted to purchasing long-lived equipment be classified?
choices: Operating activities
Investing activities
Noncash disclosure only
Financing activities
exp: Cash contributions restricted for long-term purposes, such as acquiring long-lived assets or establishing an endowment, are financing inflows (ASC 230-10-45-14). Investing is tempting because equipment is involved, but the later purchase is the investing outflow, not the gift.

q: During Year 1, Spruce Alliance received unconditional pledges of $250,000, of which 8% are expected to be uncollectible. It also received a $40,000 pledge contingent on Spruce obtaining a matching federal grant, which it has not yet obtained. What total contribution revenue from pledges should Spruce recognize in Year 1?
exp: Unconditional pledges are recognized net of estimated uncollectibles: $250,000 x 92% = $230,000; the $40,000 pledge is conditional and is not recognized until the barrier is overcome. The $270,000 answer wrongly includes the conditional pledge.

q: How should an NFP report expenses, including those funded by donor-restricted gifts, in its statement of activities?
choices: In the net asset class that provided the funding
As decreases in net assets without donor restrictions
Split between the two classes based on the funding source
As decreases in net assets with donor restrictions until the restriction expires
exp: All expenses are reported as decreases in net assets without donor restrictions; restricted funding is reflected through a release from restrictions. Reporting expenses in the class that funded them is the common error.

q: Fir Society received a $25,000 gift restricted to a summer camp program and spent it on the camp in the same reporting period. Which reporting treatment is permitted?
choices: Report it as without donor restrictions only if the donor later agrees in writing
Report it as an exchange transaction because the program was delivered
Report it as without donor restrictions if the entity has a policy to do so, applies it consistently and discloses it
Report it as with donor restrictions with no release until the next period
exp: ASC 958-605-45 permits reporting restricted contributions whose restrictions are met in the same period as without donor restrictions, provided the policy is consistently applied and disclosed. Otherwise the gift is reported with donor restrictions and released in that same period, not the next.

q: How must an NFP present investment return in its statement of activities under ASU 2016-14?
choices: Gross, with investment expenses reported as management and general expenses
Gross, with investment expenses disclosed in the notes
Net of all investment expenses, with the netted amount disclosed
Net of external and direct internal investment expenses, with no requirement to disclose the netted expenses
exp: ASU 2016-14 requires investment return to be presented net of external and direct internal investment expenses and eliminated the disclosure of those netted expenses. Gross presentation with investment expenses in management and general is no longer appropriate.

q: A museum acquires a painting for public exhibition. The painting will be protected and preserved, and museum policy requires proceeds from sales of collection items to be used to acquire other items or for their direct care. What is the museum's accounting option?
choices: It may elect not to capitalize the item as part of a collection
It must capitalize the painting at cost and depreciate it
It must capitalize the painting and test it for impairment annually
It must expense the painting as program services in all cases
exp: Items meeting the definition of a collection may be left uncapitalized under ASC 958-360, with required disclosures; the ASU 2019-03 direct-care language is included in that definition. Works of art are not depreciated even when capitalized, so the depreciation answer is wrong.

q: Which presentation of net assets is required on an NFP's statement of financial position?
choices: Three classes: unrestricted, temporarily restricted and permanently restricted
Net assets with donor restrictions and without donor restrictions shown separately, along with total net assets
A single total net assets amount, with classes disclosed only in the notes
Separate funds for each restricted gift received during the year
exp: ASU 2016-14 replaced the three classes with two, with donor restrictions and without donor restrictions, which are shown on the face along with total net assets. The three-class model is the superseded presentation.
